description: We are a team of two engineering students from ENSAM Meknès — one specializing in Software Engineering and Intelligent Systems, and the other in AI and Data Science. We're looking for new members to bring additional value to the team.
summary:
EarthEyes is an end-to-end autonomous agro-climate intelligence platform built for the Adapting Farms with NASA Data Challenge. We developed an agentic AI system — powered by Gemini 2.5 Flash — that fuses 42 years of NASA POWER daily climatology, NASA SMAP topsoil moisture, and NASA SRTM 30m elevation data with biophysical crop modeling (WOFOST), Random Forest yield prediction, and computer vision leaf pathology diagnosis to deliver precision farming decisions.

The platform directly addresses Morocco's compounding agricultural crisis: six consecutive drought years, a spring rainfall decline of 21.4%, and smallholder over-reliance on monoculture bread wheat vulnerable to Chergui heat events. Rather than passive dashboards, EarthEyes deploys an autonomous agent brain with 11 scientific tools that it dynamically orchestrates — selecting the right combination of NASA telemetry, soil analysis, terrain modeling, and crop simulations — to produce grounded, farm-specific rotation recommendations in quintals, water savings in m³, and fertilizer economics in Moroccan Dirhams.
details:
Project Overview: EarthEyes is an autonomous agro-climatic intelligence and crop rotation platform designed to help smallholder farmers adapt to intensifying climate volatility in semi-arid basins, piloted in the Saïss Plain (Meknès, Morocco). By fusing 41 years of NASA Earth Observations with biophysical growth simulation and conversational AI, EarthEyes provides smallholders with optimal, climate-resilient crop rotation pathways that break vulnerable cereal monocultures, protect depleted groundwater, and restore soil fertility.

1. What does it do and how does it work? EarthEyes operates as a two-state decision engine with an intuitive, biophilic interface. The system ingests 41 years of continuous daily weather data from the NASA POWER API (1984–2025), segmenting the data into two 21-year climatic eras (1984–2003 vs. 2004–2025) to quantify localized climate disruption (+0.53°C warming anomaly and a -9.4% drop in crucial spring rainfall). It integrates NASA SMAP surface volumetric soil moisture (0–5 cm) to verify seedbed germination readiness (optimal 12%–18%), NASA SRTM 30m for topographic slope and erosion runoff modeling, Sentinel-2 NDVI for canopy vigor, and ISRIC SoilGrids for vertisol clay and pH mapping. Using modified WOFOST crop phenology and Random Forest modeling, EarthEyes simulates multi-season yields and ranks resilient rotation candidates based on a multi-criteria Agro-Ecological Score. The farmer inputs three basic fields (current crop, acreage, and water regime). In one click, EarthEyes displays the optimal recommendation (#1 Hero crop) with exactly three critical metrics (yield, water saved, nitrogen fixed), accompanied by practical local agronomic advice and an autonomous Gemini 2.5 Agronomist drawer.

2. What benefits does it have? EarthEyes promotes financial stability by preventing harvest collapse from spring heatwaves (Chergui) through diversification into early-maturing or drought-hardy crops (e.g., chickpea, rustic faba bean, spring sunflower). It supports groundwater conservation by saving between 620 m³ to 1,800 m³ of irrigation water per hectare, easing pressure on the over-exploited Saïss aquifer (which declines by 1.5 m annually). It also enables natural soil regeneration, as legume rotations introduce symbiotic biological nitrogen fixation (+35 to +45 kg N/ha), reducing synthetic fertilizer costs and greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, it contributes to disease cycle disruption by breaking soil-borne pathogen cycles (such as wheat foot rot and take-all fungi), reducing pesticide dependency.

3. What is the intended impact of the project? EarthEyes aims to strengthen local resilience by empowering smallholder family farmers in Morocco’s breadbasket with actionable scientific data that was previously locked behind academic and institutional barriers. While validated in the Saïss basin, its open architecture is designed for global scalability across semi-arid Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and sub-Saharan agro-ecosystems facing climate-induced drought. It also promotes open science democratization by bridging the digital divide and translating NASA raw telemetry into plain language (English, French, and Modern Standard Arabic).

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? The backend and simulation infrastructure relies on Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, and the PCSE/WOFOST crop simulation engine. For AI and reasoning, EarthEyes uses Google Gemini 2.5 Flash for the autonomous Agronomic Agent, augmented with RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) grounded in Moroccan INRA and FAO crop rotation guidelines. Its satellite and environmental data sources include NASA POWER API, NASA SMAP L3/L4, NASA SRTM 30m, Copernicus Sentinel-2, and ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0. The frontend and user experience are built with Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5/CSS3 (custom design system with zero heavy framework bloat), Leaflet.js for interactive GIS geolocation, and Web Speech API for voice dictation. Cloudflare Tunnel provides secure, instant worldwide HTTPS edge distribution.

5. How is your project creative? EarthEyes moves away from dark, aggressive "neon-dashboard" aesthetics toward a warm paper palette (#F6F4EC) and natural moss-green hues inspired by agronomy, prioritizing visual calmness for farmers under climate stress. It features native Standard Arabic (RTL) integration with a full right-to-left layout and pure Arabic script, eliminating unreadable Latin transliterations. Instead of focusing solely on yield, its Agro-Ecological Scoring system recognizes that maximum gross tonnage can be dangerous under water scarcity and ranks crops according to sustainability, water productivity, and net resilient margins. Finally, its "Farmer’s Insight" integration preserves traditional agrarian wisdom through soft quote highlights alongside high-tech satellite metrics.

6. What factors did your team consider? EarthEyes accounts for cognitive load and digital literacy, recognizing that rural farmers cannot navigate complex multi-variable dashboards; therefore, it compresses deep astrophysics and agro-climate models into a clean 3-control input and 1-click output. It also addresses low-bandwidth conditions and network instability through a lightweight frontend architecture without heavy frameworks, using system fallback typography and pre-cached telemetry. Regarding climatic historical depth, the project recognizes that a 5-year weather baseline is insufficient under climate change and that only a 41-year span captures true decadal aridification trends in North Africa. Finally, it considers soil physics and vertisol dynamics by factoring in the high clay content (36%+) of Saïss soils, where improper crop selection leads to compaction and severe percolation failure.
